sections.title: Employment Contract
sections.text:
Defender Operator Mechanist, joining your command roster effective today.

In truth, though, you were placed in his chain of command long ago. After all, so many of the devices you've used were created by him — and are controlled by him.

sections.title: Token
sections.text: A bottle of liquor. The drink itself hardly matters, of course — what matters is the technological marvel he'll show you once he's drunk: the embodiment of all his thoughts and feelings, or in Logos's words, "his soul." For now? Just drink.

sections.title: Profile
sections.text: Mechanist, Elite Operator of Rhodes Island. He leads the research, manufacture, and maintenance of Rhodes Island's weaponry, engineering facilities, and laboratory equipment, providing the hardware support that operators in every department require.

sections.title: Clinical Analysis
sections.text:
Imaging tests show the indistinct outlines of internal organs, obscured by abnormal shadows. Originium granules detected in the circulatory system. The subject is confirmed to be infected with Oripathy.

[Cell-Originium Assimilation] 5%
Small amounts of Originium crystals can be observed on the surface of Operator Mechanist's body.

[Blood Originium-Crystal Density] 0.17u/L
Operator Mechanist adheres strictly to the most rigorous protective protocols, and rarely removes his work suit even outside of work.

'Now you know what a dangerous hobby mechanical engineering is.'
—Mechanist

sections.title: Archive File 1
sections.text:
Mechanist almost never takes off his work suit.
Not that anyone actually wants to see that weed-patch of hair, or the eyes that grow and shrink with his lack of sleep—but when he sits down at the dinner table still wearing the suit, we can't help wondering all the same.
'So he can get to work at a moment's notice' was our first guess. It isn't hard to imagine the despair of someone struck by a brilliant idea only to find that he must first complete the whole tedious ritual of suiting up at the laboratory door.
But for someone with Mechanist's skills, building a rig to get him in and out of the suit quickly would hardly be difficult—certainly not difficult enough to justify enduring all the inconveniences of never taking it off.
Only later did we learn that he wasn't 'enduring' any inconvenience at all.
Restricted movement? The concealed wheels and jet canisters in his soles beg to differ.
Too hot inside? The built-in air conditioning, fans, and cooling patches take care of that.
What about scratching an itch? Inside the suit there is a small mechanical hand at the front and another at the back, sliding up and down on rails to reach every inch of skin except the soles of his feet.
And what about showing his face? Everyone ought to have seen the displays he sewed into that suit—scrolling Columbian profanity—back when he returned to Columbia after all those years, on a mission that just so happened to require him to walk in and out of Volvort Kochinski's headquarters.
That single layer of work suit converts a great many problems into the kind Mechanist is best at solving—the kind that can be solved by mechanical means.
Praise him for it and he will politely reply that he is simply doing things his own way. You won't see his expression, but you will hear the little mechanical hand inside the suit scratching his head for him.

sections.title: Archive File 2
sections.text:
When Mechanist first turned up at our gatherings, he was not yet an Elite Operator.
那不算是我们最好过的时候，哪怕在开聚会也没几个人开心得起来，从Misery脸上就看得出——他会为此感到抱歉，但每次对事情感到悲观的时候，他还是会露出那种……好像所有人都命不久矣的眼神。Raidian有时会让“小树”和“小轴”牵起手，合着拍子在桌上旋转两圈，但她原来是会自己上场跳舞的。Logos偶尔还是会尝试用他那些怪异的咒言逗乐大伙儿，但他也在很小心地避免搞出太不合时宜的恶作剧。
All that was left was the sound of the radio.
It was at moments like that when Mechanist would stroll through us with his toolbox as if nothing were amiss and start fiddling with that thermometer-looking device on the wall. It was another of the things he had brought from Columbia, and it seemed to break down constantly—every time we gathered there, we would find him repairing it.
Once he started hammering away, the lyrics on the radio became impossible to make out, and instead you began to notice all sorts of other sounds—like Rhodes Island grinding over sand and gravel beneath us.
'Which one of you keeps generating heat one moment and cold the next?' he asked, turning around abruptly.
Logos glanced sheepishly at the flask in his hand, half frozen over and half still burning.
'Thermodynamics above.' He grumbled and tossed over a roll of insulating cloth.
'The days aren't over yet,' I said, watching him, the words surfacing out of nowhere. 'At least that fellow is still fixing his gadget.'
Everyone laughed.
——Ace

It was only after Mechanist joined that we gradually took up the habit of organizing all manner of games and contests.
He was a better batter than many a Rim Billitonian, and better than many a Leithanien at mimicking bits from song-and-dance variety acts. He knew every brand of cigarette card and the betting rules that went with them, and he was an expert at the puzzle games printed in science fiction magazines. How he once used all this to entertain investors, we cannot say; but we all saw for ourselves how deftly he used it to entertain himself. More often than not, he was happy to invent some absurd ruleset of his own—the Paperclip Fencing Championship, say, or the Don't-Scorch-the-Potatoes Stir-Fry Contest—and then drag everyone into his chaotic betting pool.
Depending on when the gathering fell, we might weep, laugh, make a racket, or fall silent—but Mechanist was always doing the same thing. If we weren't in the mood to play with him, he played with the Structural Principle; and if a third player was needed, he added the mechanical arm on his back.
Once the betting was over and the alcohol had spread well enough through him, he would start composing poetry—the sort of poetry you get by tossing a physics monograph into a crucible and stirring. His most recent poem ends like this:
'Whoever is continuously symmetric through the flux of time, the conserved quantity of their life is life itself.'
He so often translates my words uninvited that I ought to translate one of his poems for once. Just as a farmer whose every rule in life is set by when to sow, how to stitch, and the craft of slaughtering a cystybeast will never doubt his own life through any upheaval on this land, so too will a man whose rules of living are never broken never lose the meaning of his life.
Perhaps I should add one more joke: Mechanist has never once realized that he is exactly that sort of man.
And that genuinely puts all of us at ease. Now and then, the words surface out of nowhere for any one of us—
'The days aren't over yet—at least Mechanist is still reciting his poems.'
—Logos

sections.title: Archive File 3
sections.text:
This is my fifth year working at the Patent Bureau.
My daughter told her class again that she wants my job when she grows up. Her teacher came to tell me, so I had no choice but to offer a couple of compliments as sincerely as I could manage. After all, next time I will need to ask that teacher to hand out our questionnaires to the whole class.
Each day's work takes place in a capsule laboratory pod of less than ten square meters. The technical department sends us the patents it has screened, and we—'like children with a brand new toy'—apply those technologies to every situation we can dream up. Handed an anti-jolt bearing from a mobility scooter, why not try it as the spindle of a cotton candy machine?
That is where the questionnaires come in. We set aside everything we learned at the polytechnic and first make ourselves familiar with every need this country might possibly have. Heavens, I even know the 'class hierarchy' by which schoolchildren rank one another's stationery.
Upstairs they say we are turning a single patent nobody may ever pay for into ten or twenty 'applied patents' that are certain to reach production and turn a profit. The ownership of those 'applied patents', of course, has nothing to do with the original inventor, and nothing to do with us either—they belong to Columbia.
—A researcher at the Columbia Bureau of Thought Property and Patents

The resolution passed, and power poured into the Patent Bureau like a burst levee. Let the Bureau deal with objects; what the Patent Bureau confiscates is ideas.
A Patent Bureau enforcement agent's standard kit is two ballpoint pens, a dozen patent application forms, and a portable door breacher. With these he can pinpoint every technical design not certified by the Patent Bureau. Put it into production yourself? Illegal. Sell the blueprints? Illegal. Only use it yourself? A latent risk of illegality.
Every truly valuable design must become a patent, so that the researchers of the Patent Application Department can then multiply it into new applications many times over. Whether the inventor actually wants the 'protection' of a patent is beside the point.
One can imagine how much resentment the resolution stirred up when it first passed. The Patent Bureau urgently needed a case intimidating enough to underline its authority.
Volvort Kochinski delivered a suitable victim: an Elafia engineer so stubbornly protective of his own creations that he had fallen out with them. His workshop was turned upside down, and everything but the designs delivered to the company—the ones he had tried to produce and profit from himself, the ones he had donated to his alma mater as teaching aids, and the ones he had built for his own use—was to be confiscated in full, and he was fined a hefty sum besides.
In the end, of course, the Patent Bureau confiscated nothing at all: that Elafia fled with his blueprints to a medical enterprise beyond the borders. But that only let the Bureau trumpet his suspicious identity and impure motives far and wide, and thereby cement the righteousness of its confiscations.

[A Request for Landship Leave]
Once the adaptive climate control system is officially in service aboard this ship as well, I will return to Columbia.
My thanks to your company: every technology I brought has been put to proper use, which means the purpose of my coming here has been fully accomplished.
I am well aware that returning to Columbia is dangerous for me, but my instincts are pushing me to attend to another side of the matter.
Many people liken a nation to a machine, either to declare a political stance or to level a political critique. But after this, I truly can feel it clearly—
Columbia is a machine.
我依然不会对它有半分认可，但它的运作逻辑……有着那种独属于机械的纯粹理性和效率。我是不是其中的受害者，都不影响这一点。我不喜欢阴谋论，但如果现在有人说这个国家的运作在根基上确实是由一台机器推动的，我不会感到奇怪。
I am curious.

This request was left pressed beneath Mechanist's workbench and never submitted to the HR Department.

sections.title: Archive File 4
sections.text:
[Excerpt from a Non-Objective Profile, p.04]
Mechanist did indeed once think about leaving Rhodes Island and returning to Columbia. Back then, he had not yet met Whitesmith.
Whitesmith sought him out herself. Mechanist's first words to her were to ask why she had not replaced her wheelchair with a powered one, when she was perfectly capable of building it.
An understanding between geniuses, I suppose. He did not need to know her to see that her veins ran with molten iron, and she did not need to have met him to guess that his head was full of gears. Whitesmith understood her own condition, and understood that Rhodes Island's workshop needed a successor—and Mechanist had arrived at exactly the right moment.
What she had not anticipated was how spectacularly bad Mechanist was at the job. When he first took over the maintenance and manufacture of the elite operators' equipment, not one of his creations was usable. A composite bow he had spent three days polishing came apart in Stormeye's hands within three minutes, and the snapped bowstring nearly took off half of Stormeye's horn.
The next day, a plastic crate appeared outside Mechanist's workshop with a bottle of whiskey in it. For a while after that, Mechanist never left the workshop, and each day another bottle appeared in the crate by the door. Mechanist never drinks during working hours; he said these were being saved for after he had solved the problem. When that day came, he would make up in one go for every drink he had wanted but had no chance to have.
It is not hard to understand why he was so obsessive. Even with his helmet always on, everyone could tell: the truth he had believed without question for over twenty years had shattered aboard Rhodes Island. He could not grasp why his perfect designs, seemingly the very incarnation of physical law, looked so crude in the hands of the elite operators. He iterated on them at a rate of five drafts a day—and still, of course, the results were not what he wanted.
Taking over someone else's engineering, and tuning machines to the measure of a person, were both still far too unfamiliar to him at the time. He did not yet understand that what those less-than-by-the-book elite operators actually needed was only a little of the odd, deliberate 'flaw'.

[Excerpt from a Non-Objective Profile, p.11]
By then Whitesmith's condition had grown very poor, and the workshop was already run entirely by Mechanist. But one day, she suddenly said she wanted to forge something again.
She lit the forge for the first time in a long while, meaning only to repair someone's weapon—but Mechanist told her that every repair request had already been handled. This last time, he wanted Whitesmith's forge to burn for no one but herself.
Every piece of equipment she would use, Mechanist had modified to exactly the right degree: each step still had to be done by hand, but each could be completed with only the smallest of movements. Even Whitesmith, who by then struggled just to move her arms, could work them.
For one small pendant, Whitesmith forged from day into night and from night into day again—but sincerity and perseverance were the two things she never lacked. Mechanist watched from the side the whole time; he knew that however long it took, this was something only her own hands could finish.
At last, when the pendant was finished, Mechanist shaved away one facet of the gemstone. The light it cast would never again fall perfectly at its center—but only that way did it look more like Whitesmith's eyes.
After that, Whitesmith's forge never burned again. That night, Mechanist drank every bottle outside the workshop door by himself.

'The first time we met, I asked her why she didn't replace her wheelchair with a powered one. She said it was because her hands could still move.
'That is my reason for staying at Rhodes Island.'
—Mechanist

sections.title: Promotion Record
sections.text:
Yes, this is the Structural Principle, Mechanist's proudest creation.
It is nowhere near as cute as it looks. We rarely describe a machine as 'fiercely territorial', but for the Structural Principle no phrase could fit better. The Engineering Department's vehicle bay never used to have assigned spaces—Bagpipe's little tractor, Earthspirit's sidecar motorcycle, those few autonomous work platforms, all parked wherever they pleased—until the Structural Principle came along. Nobody knows how it settled on that particular space, but the moment anyone approaches it, the thing stiffens its neck, takes an attacking stance, and drives the intruder off.
Sober, Mechanist refuses to admit that the Structural Principle, being a machine, has any personality to speak of—but everyone knows why it has the personality it has. Just as he never realizes that all his poems describe himself, he will never realize how much the Structural Principle resembles him.
Yes—Mechanist is himself a 'fiercely territorial' man. At first, his 'territory' held only the immovable laws of physics and all those proud creations he would let no one else touch. But by now he could no longer say what his 'territory' contains: it has gained people he cares about, principles he has come to accept, and perhaps a few things he wants to accomplish.
If he was once willing to defy the federal government's penalty order without regard for the consequences just to protect his own creations, then now, for the people and things he cares about, he will surely not give ground by so much as half a step.

'Like how he wrote twenty layers of defense routines into the Structural Principle?'
'Like how the Structural Principle stands with its neck stiffened, guarding its parking space.'
